challenges.name: revocation-quiz
challenges.title: When does a signed-out session really stop?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the stolen-laptop ticket: an access token that still worked after the family was revoked, and how long a deny-list entry has to live.

questions.question:
POST /sessions/revoke-all (14:02) ran:

UPDATE refresh_tokens SET revoked_at = now()
 WHERE user_id = 'u_5521' AND revoked_at IS NULL;   -- 3 rows

The access guard only verifies the signature and exp. API log afterwards:

14:06:40 GET /courses/42/progress  200  sid=fam_812 iat=14:01:30 exp=14:16:30
14:12:10 GET /me/certificates       200  sid=fam_812 iat=14:01:30 exp=14:16:30
14:16:40 GET /me/certificates       401  token_expired
14:16:41 POST /auth/refresh         401  refresh_token_revoked

Statement: "The laptop kept access until 14:16 because revoking the refresh-token rows does nothing to an access token that was already issued; to stop it earlier, the guard has to check something per request, such as the user's session version or a deny list of revoked families."
questions.explanation: True. An access token is self-contained: the guard checked the signature and exp, both fine until 14:16:30, and never looked at refresh_tokens. Revoking the rows only blocked the next refresh, which is exactly what the 14:16:41 line shows. To cut those 14 minutes, the guard needs a cheap per-request check: the token's ver claim against users.session_version (bumped by sign-out-all), or its sid against a deny list of revoked families. The misconception is that revoking a session in the database revokes the tokens already handed out.

False. After the UPDATE, the family can never refresh again, so no new access token is issued for it. Every access token it already has was issued before the revocation and expires at most 15 minutes later. An entry that lives 15 minutes (the access token lifetime, plus your allowed clock skew) covers all of them; after that the exp check rejects them by itself. Keeping entries for 14 days only makes the deny list grow with every sign-out, which is the cost you wanted to bound. The misconception is to tie the deny list to the refresh token lifetime instead of the access token lifetime.

challenges.name: sign-out-one-device-or-all
challenges.title: Sign out one device or all devices
challenges.description:
The Settings page of https://app.codedev.test gets a Sessions section: a list of the learner's devices, "Sign out" next to each one, and "Sign out of all devices", which the password change also triggers. A session is a refresh token family: one familyId per sign-in on one device, rows shaped like { id, familyId, userId, deviceId, tokenHash, createdAt, expiresAt, usedAt, revokedAt, replacedBy }. Access tokens live 15 minutes (ACCESS_TTL_MS) and carry the decoded claims { sub, sid, ver, iat, exp }: sub = userId, sid = familyId, ver = the user's session version when the token was issued. Sign-in and rotation (with replay detection) are already written; write the five functions they rely on.

revokeFamily(s, userId, familyId, now): if no row of familyId belongs to userId (unknown family or another user's), return false and change nothing. Otherwise set revokedAt = now on every row of the family whose revokedAt is null; if at least one row changed, put the family on the deny list with s.deniedFamilies.set(familyId, now + ACCESS_TTL_MS). Return true (also for a family that was already revoked).

signOutAll(s, userId, now): bump the user's session version (s.sessionVersion, a missing user counts as 0) by 1, set revokedAt = now on every row of the user whose revokedAt is null, and add nothing to the deny list.

checkAccess(s, claims, now) runs on every API request and may use only the two maps, never s.rows: now >= claims.exp -> "expired"; claims.ver lower than the user's session version -> "revoked"; claims.sid on the deny list -> "revoked"; otherwise "ok".

pruneDenyList(s, now): delete every deny-list entry whose time is <= now. The runner calls it before every operation, so the list only holds families revoked in the last 15 minutes.

listSessions(s, userId, now): one entry per family of the user that has a live row (usedAt null, revokedAt null, now < expiresAt), with its deviceId, createdAt = the smallest createdAt of the family's rows and lastUsedAt = the largest. Sort by lastUsedAt, newest first, then by familyId ascending (plain string comparison).

Input: a JSON list of operations in time order, with "at" in minutes on a fake clock (login, refresh, api, logout, revoke, logoutAll, passwordChanged, sessions, denylist; see the test runner). Output: one line per operation. Times are whole minutes; up to 1000 operations.
hints: Revoking rows in the table stops the next refresh. What stops an access token that was issued two minutes before the sign-out, and how long does that thing need to remember the family?

Look at what each operation must change: revokeFamily touches the family's rows and the deny list, signOutAll touches the user's rows and the session version, checkAccess only reads the two maps. In listSessions, group the user's rows by familyId before you decide whether a family is live.

A similar case on other data: a course pass is revoked at minute 40 and passes are valid for 10 minutes, so an entry in a revoked-passes map with time 40 + 10 = 50 is enough; at minute 50 the pass has expired by itself and the entry can go. A user-wide counter does the same job for "revoke everything": passes that carry an older counter value are rejected, with no entry per pass.
